title: Many names for a bowl
hookLine: don't insist on your local word; a bowl has many names
last: NEITHER FLIES OFF NOR HOLDS ON.

cards: Soda. Pop. Coke, even when it isn't.
Sneakers or tennis shoes. Some people have argued about these words at a family reunion with real heat.
The hundred and thirty-ninth discourse is about living without conflict, and much of it is about big things: pleasure and self-torment, praise and blame, how to speak.
But tucked inside is a small, almost funny example about tableware. The same simple bowl, the Buddha notices, goes by different names in different districts.

teach.b: The discourse is called the exposition of non-conflict, araṇa. It lists ways to live without stirring up conflict. Don't pursue sensual pleasure, and don't torment yourself: the middle way.
Know what praise and blame are, and teach without either. Don't say things in secret that would hurt if known, or speak harshly to someone's face.
Speak unhurriedly, because hurried speech tires the body and the mind, and is hard to follow. And: don't insist on local language, and don't override ordinary usage. Here's the example.
In one district, people call a bowl pati. In another, patta. In others, still other names.

Someone who clings to their own district's word says: only this is correct, everything else is wrong. That, the text says, is insisting on local language and overriding ordinary usage, a path with conflict in it.
The other person, wherever they go, thinks: it seems these people call it this. And speaks as they do, without grasping. That's the path without conflict.
A teaching about freedom stops to talk about kitchen words, and it fits. Some fights aren't about the thing at all; they're about whose name for it wins.
The monastic rules have a related passage, and readers disagree about it: some hear the Buddha letting monks learn his words in their own dialects; the old commentary hears his own language.
A bowl holds rice whatever it's called. The text ends by naming a monk, Subhuti, as one who walked this way of non-conflict.

how: Buddhist teachings are chanted and studied in Pali, Sanskrit, Chinese, Tibetan, Japanese, English and other languages; a Vinaya passage on learning the Buddha's words in one's own dialect is read differently by different schools and scholars.

o: a monk's bowl used for collecting alms
the one true name for a thing

games.q: the way of non-conflict: tap the pairs.
p: different districts' words for a bowl

s: in MN 139 the Buddha says the people of one district have the correct word for bowl
he says insisting on one district's word is the path with conflict in it.
hurried speech tires the body and mind and is hard to follow.
MN 139 names Subhuti as one who walked the way of non-conflict
the discourse ends by naming him.

games.q: you arrive in a new district. people there call your bowl by a word you've never used. what does MN 139 suggest?
o: think, it seems they call it this, and speak as they do.
refuse to use any word for it.
games.why: the one without conflict doesn't grasp at local usage; they speak as the people there speak.

practice: Think of a word, a name or a pronunciation you've corrected someone about, or wanted to: a term for God, a holiday, a dish.
Picture them saying it their way, notice any little push to fix it, and let the push soften: it seems they call it this. Let the breath be unhurried.

wordCard.voice: Arana. Without conflict: don't insist your local word, like pati or patta, is the only right one; speak as people speak, without grasping. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali arana: without conflict, without strife. the title of MN 139.

carryVoice: Your line: speak as people speak. Pati or patta, it's still a bowl. Day five hundred five, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 139, Aranavibhanga Sutta (the exposition of non-conflict)
Vinaya, Cullavagga V.33 (learning the teaching in one's own language)
